newsitem.title: ITALY: Carnival sees cruise expansion, views Asia.
newsitem.headline: Carnival sees cruise expansion, views Asia.

text.p: Carnival Corp sees continued success and major expansion for its cruise lines with particular focus on the Asian market, company officials said on Thursday.

Chief executive Micky Arison and other officials were speaking to reporters in Venice on the occasion of the official launch of the more than 100,000 gross ton Carnival Destiny, the biggest cruise ship ever built.

"There is no question this new ship will be a great success. Bookings are already excellent for its maiden cruise in the Caribbean in November," Arison told Reuters in an interview on the ship, moored in the Venice lagoon.
The $400 million cruise liner was built in just 20 months by Italy's state shipbuilder Fincantieri at its dockyard in the northeastern port of Trieste.
"We are the largest cruise liner in the world and the most profitable," said Bob Dickinson, President of Carnival Cruise Lines, a division of Carnival Corp.
Carnival Corp reported net income of $268.1 million and $0.92 earnings per share for the third quarter ended August 31 1996, compared to $209.5 million and $0.74 EPS in the year ago period.
Analyst forecasts for the fourth quarter of this year are for $0.38 earnings per share.
"The fourth quarter is always the toughest for the industry," Arison said, but added the cruise line business was on track to post record results again this year.

Howard Frank, chief financial officer of Carnival Corp, said its move in April to take a 30 percent stake in Airtours Plc, a major tour operator in the UK and Scandinavia, had been a very successful investment.
"Our visibility this side of the Atlantic has very noticably increased," he added.

Arison said: "We see the market globalising, cruising everywhere with passengers from everywhere, from the primary North American market to Europe and the Far East. The company's most recent joint venture is with South Korea's Hyundai Corp and it plans to start cruising in Asia in 1998.

Dickinson said cruising only captured two percent of the tourism market in North America. The company has a more than 35 percent share of the North American cruise market in terms of passengers carried and expects it to be close to 40 percent in 1996-97.

"The Asian market, particularly the western part of the Pacific rim is virtually an untapped market. There are very few players there and the Australian market has not been tapped at all. We are aiming for a larger share here," Dickinson said.

Frank said the Carnival Destiny was the first of seven ships commissioned by the group over the next three years. "We are therefore confident of our ability to grow business in North America and Asia."
The deal with Hyundai involved selling Carnival's Tropical cruise liner to a new joint company Carnival Hyundai, in which each partner would hold a half share.
Arison said Carnival had not yet decided whether the new company would acquire a new fleet of ships or use existing vessels for the planned Asian expansion.
